Subject: Northbridge Financial – security questionnaire follow-up (SIEM export / audit logs)

Hi Aisha,

Thanks again for the security review yesterday.

We’re finalizing our questionnaire (attached) and have a few follow-ups specifically on audit logs / SIEM export:

1) Audit log completeness: what categories of events are included (admin actions, API key changes, role changes, model deployment changes, user logins, etc.)? Are inference requests/responses included?

2) Retention: how long do you retain audit events in your system, and can we control/extend retention? (We target 7 years on our side.)

3) SIEM export: you mentioned a beta export to Splunk. What’s the delivery guarantee (exactly-once vs at-least-once), and do events have a stable unique ID we can use to dedupe?

4) Encryption/KMS: is the audit log data encrypted at rest with a customer-managed key? If we export to S3, can we require SSE-KMS with our CMK? How do you store credentials/tokens for export destinations?

If you can point us to any written FAQ or schema reference, that would help us close this out by end of week.

Best,
Jordan

—
Jordan Keller
Director, Security Architecture
Northbridge Financial

Aisha — quick bullets you can use. Kevin can add connector details.

1) Audit log completeness / categories
- Scope: security- and admin-relevant actions in the Redwood control plane + Console (e.g., user authentication events, workspace/tenant membership changes, RBAC/role changes, API key create/revoke/rotate, destination/export config changes, policy changes, and other privileged admin actions).
- We do NOT log full inference prompts/completions as “audit” events; audit is metadata about actions. (We also avoid collecting customer content in audit logs.)
- Each audit event includes: event_id, timestamp, actor (user/service), tenant/workspace, action/event_type, target resource, request_id/trace correlation fields, and IP/user agent when applicable.

2) Delivery semantics / dedupe
- Export pipeline is at-least-once. Duplicates are possible (e.g., retry after transient sink error). Each event has a stable event_id suitable for deduplication downstream.
- Ordering is best-effort; no global ordering guarantee across partitions.

3) Config changes are audited
- Any changes to export destinations/filters/credentials are themselves captured as audit events (so you can see who changed where logs are going).

GRC note: avoid promising “exactly-once” or “complete absence of duplicates”. We should message at-least-once + dedupe guidance.

-Marcus

Adding connector / crypto specifics:

SIEM export sinks (beta): Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs intake, and S3.

- Encryption in transit: TLS (HTTPS) to Splunk HEC and Datadog endpoints. We require TLS 1.2+.

- Credential storage: destination tokens/keys are stored encrypted at rest in our secrets store using envelope encryption backed by cloud KMS. Access is restricted to the export service identity and audited.

- S3 sink encryption:
  - Supports SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS.
  - For SSE-KMS, customer provides the KMS key ARN (CMK) and bucket policy; we write objects using that CMK.
  - Objects are written with deterministic naming + partitions (tenant/date/hour) to enable downstream processing; duplicates can occur under retries (at-least-once).

- Splunk HEC behavior:
  - Optional HEC ACK support (if enabled on the Splunk side) to reduce “unknown delivery state” scenarios.
  - Retries are exponential backoff on 429/5xx; auth errors (401/403) are treated as terminal until credentials are updated.

Retention (Olga may want to phrase this): Console is not intended as long-term archival; for long retention we recommend export to customer-controlled storage/SIEM.

Kevin

Aisha — for retention + KMS wording, recommend the following (customer-safe) language:

- Audit events are retained within the Redwood service for a limited operational period; customers who require longer retention should export to their SIEM/object storage where they control retention policies (e.g., 7 years).

- At-rest encryption: Redwood encrypts audit data and configuration data at rest using industry-standard encryption; key management is handled via cloud KMS in Hosted/Dedicated deployments. For S3 export, customer can enforce SSE-KMS with their own CMK and bucket policies.

- For Private deployments, customers control their infrastructure, including storage encryption and key management.

Avoid making commitments about specific retention durations unless we confirm what’s contractually offered for this account.

Olga

Hi Jordan,

Following up with written responses to your four questions below. (Assuming Hosted API + Dedicated capacity; if you move to Private/VPC later, you control storage and key management end-to-end.)

1) Audit log completeness / categories
- Our audit events cover security- and admin-relevant actions in the Redwood control plane + Console, including (non-exhaustive): user authentication events, workspace/tenant membership changes, RBAC/role changes, API key create/revoke/rotate, configuration changes impacting security posture, and changes to audit export destinations/filters.
- Audit logs are designed for SIEM correlation and do not include customer inference payload content (prompts/completions) as part of audit events.
- Events include fields such as: event_id, timestamp, tenant/workspace, actor identity, event_type/action, target resource identifiers, and correlation IDs (e.g., request_id). IP/user agent are included where applicable.

2) Retention
- Redwood retains audit events inside the service for a limited operational period (not intended as long-term archive).
- For 7-year retention requirements, we recommend exporting to your SIEM/object storage where you control retention policies.

3) SIEM export (beta) delivery guarantee + dedupe
- Delivery semantics are at-least-once (duplicates are possible under retries).
- Each audit event includes a stable unique event_id suitable for downstream deduplication.
- Ordering is best-effort; there is no global ordering guarantee across partitions/destinations.

4) Encryption/KMS + credential handling
- Data is encrypted in transit to supported sinks (HTTPS/TLS).
- Configuration and destination credentials (e.g., Splunk HEC token / Datadog API key) are stored encrypted at rest, with envelope encryption backed by cloud KMS; access is restricted to the exporter service identity and audited.
- For S3 export, we support SSE-KMS and you can require use of your CMK via bucket/KMS key policies.

I’m attaching a draft customer-facing FAQ for SIEM export and a short excerpt of our Audit Event Schema v1 (for field names + types). If you’d like, we can also jump on a 20-min call with your Splunk team to align on parsing + dedupe.

Best,
Aisha

—
Aisha Rahman
Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference

From: Aisha Rahman <aisha@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Mon, Feb 10, 2025 at 6:47 PM
Subject: Re: Northbridge Financial – security questionnaire follow-up (SIEM export / audit logs)

Hi Jordan,

Yes on both:

1) Export config change auditing
- Changes to audit export configuration (create/update/delete destinations, enable/disable, filter changes, credential updates) are themselves recorded as audit events, including actor identity + timestamp + the resource that was changed.

2) S3 SSE-KMS / least privilege
- SSE-KMS is configured per S3 destination, and you can specify the CMK ARN for that destination.
- We support operating with least-privilege IAM (typical: s3:PutObject to a scoped prefix and kms:Encrypt / kms:GenerateDataKey on the specified key). Your bucket + key policies can enforce these constraints.

If you send me the specific questionnaire rows you want mapped to these answers, I can paste exact language into the cells as well.

Best,
Aisha
